At night in Brooklyn, the tendrils of a white sex denuded the sky, shimmering at the tall needle- ends of buildings. The traffic was identical in the spring. outputs.L2: Weather processes reality through its joints. Music exhales whenever a wound splits open. When I unlatch a gate, the hue beneath rooftops and branches becomes mine. From you came the final quartets, one dark bird, one pale bird, and Eden itself. Your dying belongs to everyone except me. I question things so memory won't fail me. Nighttime Brooklyn revealed white sexual filaments unfurling across the sky, glinting at the sharp spires of skyscrapers. Spring traffic repeated itself without variation. Only forgotten melodies shield me. Why do the sharpest intellects eventually turn to writing fables? Death multiplies. Fresh creatures emerge everywhere, carrying the scent of organs. The mating season's schedule concludes. Countless new moths appear, and death can no longer be glimpsed by a girl of maybe twelve, watching sideways, as if what's coming were merely a man's cuff or gait. I ask questions to keep a farmhouse supper from finishing. We gathered around a squat table. Our hostess was approaching death without knowing it—tomorrow she'd be killed in some faraway city. Something exists beyond language that isn't quiet. Something exists beyond God that isn't loneliness—a house pet instructing a dying woman in the art of the hunt. A wound splits open. A gate swings wide. Vines ascend.

# On the Thresholds of Knowing: Body, Death, and the Language Beyond Silence

There exists a mode of understanding that bypasses the intellect entirely, residing instead in the body's own strange wisdom. The image of a climate that "thinks with its knees" captures this perfectly—an intelligence rooted not in the mind but in joints, in physical sensation, in the accumulated knowledge of matter moving through space and time. This is knowledge felt rather than reasoned, understood through the body's unconventional faculties. Similarly, when music seems to "suspire" as wounds open, we witness breath and pain merging into something like song—suffering itself becoming a kind of exhalation, a rhythm that emerges not from composition but from the body's raw response to injury. Both images insist that meaning need not travel through rational channels; it can arrive through the knee, through the wound, through means we have not been trained to recognize as legitimate ways of knowing.

This theme of hidden revelation extends into the spatial imagery of gates and openings, thresholds that, once crossed or glimpsed through, disclose colors and possibilities otherwise concealed. Such openings become the site of connection—between the speaker and gifts received from another: the transcendent artistry of the late quartets, the wild freedom of birds, the mythic resonance of the Garden of Eden. These gifts, disparate in origin, are unified by their arrival through liminal space. They suggest that what is most precious cannot be approached directly but must be received sideways, through a gap in the ordinary, a door left ajar between one consciousness and another.

Death, too, refuses simple containment in this vision. Rather than an ending, it appears as something pervasive and strangely generative—swarming with new life, embodied in the sudden profusion of butterflies that seem to rise from decay itself. Death transforms rather than merely terminates. Yet this transformation carries its own tragedy: the young and the innocent remain blind to this constant presence, moving through a world saturated with mortality without perceiving its weight or its strange beauty. Their unknowing is not peace but a kind of exile from a truth that surrounds them unseen.

This gap between innocence and catastrophe finds its sharpest expression in the image of a woman's impending murder, unforeseen and unmarked, set against the utter ordinariness of a shared meal. The horror lies precisely in this juxtaposition—the banality of eating together, the small rituals of nourishment and companionship, existing mere moments before violence irrevocably alters everything. This unsettling proximity between the mundane and the tragic reveals how thin the membrane is between safety and catastrophe, how little warning the ordinary world offers before it fractures.

And yet, even in the face of such rupture, there remains an insistence that language and spirituality possess an "outside"—some dimension that exceeds silence, that persists beyond the isolation death threatens to impose. This is illustrated with quiet power through the image of a domestic animal instinctively guiding a dying woman, an act requiring no words, no theological justification, only presence and instinct working in concert. In this moment, connection reveals itself as something that need not depend on speech or even on the certainty of divine attention. Even when words fail, even when God seems absent, something continues to reach toward the dying, to accompany them—proof that isolation is not the final word, that some form of communion persists at the very edges of articulable meaning.
outputs.L4:
**What the Static Remembers**

The host does not know yet. She is pouring wine into glasses that catch the neon bleeding through venetian blinds, and somewhere in the pipes beneath her floor a clock is already counting backward. This is how mercy works sometimes—by keeping us blind to our own ending, by letting us set the table one more time.

*

My grandmother's hands smelled like rosin and burnt sugar. When she died, I found her violin still tuned, as if she'd expected to return for it. The strings held their pitch for three days after—I know because I plucked them each morning, waiting for the sound to slacken into grief. It never did. Some tensions outlive the body that created them.

*

The city at 3 AM is a throat trying to swallow itself. Streetlights blink in morse code nobody translates anymore. A woman walks her dog past a mural of a saint whose face has been rained into abstraction—just color now, just the ghost of intention. The dog stops to smell something the woman cannot see: perhaps a wound in the sidewalk where the concrete gave way to something older, something that pulses.

*

She is still pouring the wine. In another room, a record skips on the same four bars—a saxophone reaching for a note it cannot resolve. This unresolved note is the truest thing in the house. It says: *I am here and I am also already leaving.* It says: *listen to the space between what I mean and what I can say.*

*

Gates do not always look like gates. Sometimes they are the pause between a question and its answer, the half-second when a phone rings and you almost don't pick it up. Sometimes they are tendrils of steam rising from a manhole cover, spelling nothing, meaning everything, dissolving before you can read them as prophecy.

*

My grandmother believed music was language's forgiveness—the thing we say when words have failed us, when we stand at the threshold of a hospital room and cannot form the sentence *you are dying* so instead we hum, we tap rhythm against the bed rail, we let vibration carry what vocabulary cannot hold.

*

The host refills her own glass now. Somewhere in the building, footsteps ascend a staircase she painted herself, robin's-egg blue, the color of unhatched things. She does not hear them. Or she hears them the way we hear our own heartbeat—present but unremarkable, background noise to the symphony of her evening. This not-hearing is its own kind of mercy, its own kind of gate.

*

I keep returning to the image of the violin, still tuned, still waiting. What if the strings held their pitch not from tension but from expectation—not what music was, but what music was *about to become*. This is what I mean when I say meaning exists in liminal spaces: not in the note itself but in the held breath before it sounds, not in death but in the doorway death opens, briefly, before closing.

*

The saxophone finally resolves. Four notes climb somewhere the ear cannot follow, and for a moment the entire apartment building seems to lean toward that sound the way plants lean toward light they cannot name. This is not language. This is not silence. This is the third thing, the thing between, where wounds become gates and gates become passage and passage becomes—

*

She sets down her glass. Footsteps stop outside her door. Somewhere, a violin that no longer has a player to hold it continues, impossibly, humming with residual warmth, as if sound were a body that takes time to grow cold, as if music were the last held note between the isolation of a single life and whatever comes after, unfolding, tendrilled, reaching toward a name we do not yet have the tongue to speak.
outputs.L5:
# The Opening

The moment before something begins carries its own particular weight. There is a stillness to it, a held breath, as if the world itself pauses to consider what comes next.

When we speak of openings, we often think first of doors—wood or metal turning on a hinge, revealing a room we hadn't yet entered. But openings are rarely so simple. The opening of a book is not just the first page; it is the accumulated curiosity that led a hand to the shelf. The opening of a conversation is not merely the first words spoken, but the courage required to speak them at all.

The best openings do not announce themselves. They arrive quietly, almost unnoticed, and it is only later—sometimes years later—that we recognize them as the point where everything shifted. A chance meeting. An offhand remark. A door left ajar by accident.

When an opportunity presents itself, it rarely comes labeled as such. It looks, more often, like an inconvenience, a detour, an interruption to plans already made. This is perhaps why so many openings pass unnoticed. We are looking for grand gestures when the actual invitation is something smaller: a question we could ask, a risk we could take, a silence we could choose to fill.

The paradox of openings is that they require both patience and readiness. One must wait, but not passively—must stay alert to the moment when waiting is no longer the right response. When the opening comes, it rarely waits for us to feel prepared.

Perhaps this is the truest thing about beginnings: they are less about what lies ahead and more about our willingness to step through, uncertain, into whatever the opening makes possible.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist prose poem that blends fragmented images of nature, death, and memory, using short declarative sentences that don't follow a linear narrative.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Garden Keeps No Hours**

The moon is a coin in a dead man's mouth. My grandmother's hands are made of wheat. They thresh themselves in the wind that isn't there.

A fox walks backward through the orchard. This means someone is forgetting. This means the apples remember for us.

There is a door in the river. I have never opened it. My father opens it every night in a country I cannot spell.

The bees have voted to become silence. The hive agrees. Inside, gold turns to ash turns to gold. This is called mourning. This is called Tuesday.

Someone is folding the horizon like a letter never sent. The mountains lean in to read it anyway.

My mother's voice lives in the throat of a well. Drop a stone. Wait. The splash is her laughing from 1974.

The crows have learned my name. They spell it wrong on purpose. This is how the dead flirt with the living.

A field of wheat is also a funeral. A funeral is also a field of wheat. The scythe doesn't know the difference. Neither does God, probably.

I found my childhood in the belly of a fish. It was smaller than I remembered. It smelled like rain that fell before I was born.

The trees undress in October and no one is ashamed. Death wears their leaves like jewelry. Death has good taste, actually.

There is a photograph that keeps changing. Yesterday my brother stood in it. Today there is only a shadow shaped like waiting.

The owls know the location of every buried thing. They will not tell you. They only ask *who, who* as if the answer isn't already rotting sweetly beneath the roots.

Snow falls upward in the memory. This is not wrong. This is just what happens when the past gets tired of gravity.

I am planting my grandfather's teeth in the garden. By spring, something will grow that speaks only in coughs and old proverbs.

The lake has my sister's eyes today. Tomorrow it will have forgotten her completely, the way water forgets the shape of every hand that ever drowned in it.

Nothing here has an ending. Nothing here had a beginning either. The deer just keep walking through the burning house as if it were any other Tuesday, as if fire were just another kind of weather, as if none of us were made of the same disappearing thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental piece of writing in the style of John Ashbery, mixing urban imagery (like Brooklyn at night) with abstract meditations on mortality and language.
counterfactuals.output:
**Brooklyn Nocturne with Vanishing Points**

Someone has left the lights on in the past again,
and now we must live in it a little longer, the extra hour
tacked onto evening like a receipt you don't remember asking for.
Here, where the water tower leans its whole argument
against the brick, against whatever it was
you meant to say about death before the small talk
swallowed it, the way the elevated train swallows
its own screech and gives back only
a kind of hush, a lozenge of quiet
dissolving over Myrtle Avenue.

I keep meaning to write the sentence
that will explain everything, but it keeps
walking a few blocks ahead of me, hands in its pockets,
whistling something from a decade
neither of us lived through. It pauses
at the corner where the bodega's neon
buzzes like a held note nobody asked for,
and I think: this is as close as I'll get
to a definition of the soul—all that fluorescent
persistence, humming through
the folding chairs, the plastic buckets of carnations
nobody will buy tonight or any night,
though they keep blooming anyway, stupidly,
the way language keeps blooming
long after the thing it was sent to fetch
has wandered off into some other century.

The bridge, meanwhile, keeps stitching
the boroughs together with lights
that don't so much illuminate as insist,
a Morse code for "we are still here,"
though who "we" refers to
changes with every rereading,
the way a name, said enough times over a hospital bed,
stops being a name and becomes
a small boat you keep pushing out
into a river that isn't listening.

I don't want to talk about mortality directly.
It's rude, like asking a stranger
what they paid for their apartment.
Better to let it drift in sideways,
disguised as weather, as the particular gray
that settles over Fort Greene around 4 p.m.
in November, a gray that isn't sad exactly,
just thorough, the way an obituary is thorough,
listing the beloved dog, the garden,
the forty years of Sundays,
and somehow still missing
the way he laughed with his whole neck.

What I mean is: the syntax fails us
right when we need it, buckles
like a folding table at a stoop sale,
and all the words spill onto the sidewalk—
irretrievable, mismatched, some of them
still wearing price tags from a life
we can no longer afford.

And yet the night arranges itself so calmly
around the brownstones, tucking in
the stoops, the rusted gates,
the pigeons already asleep
in their small grey democracies
under the eaves, as if to say:
even this, even the not-knowing,
even the word *soul* going soft
in your mouth like a starlight mint—
even this can be furniture.
You can live among it.
You can set your coffee down
on the fact of it and watch the steam
rise like a paragraph
that changes its mind
halfway through becoming a sentence,

and this, I think, is as close as I'll get tonight
to a definition of goodbye—not
an ending, but a dimmer switch
turned so slowly
you keep believing
it's still the same light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dreamlike literary passage that repeats the motif of a "gate" and "wound" opening, weaving in references to music, quartets, and a dying woman at a farmhouse dinner.
counterfactuals.output:
The gate opens first, as gates do in dreams—without hinges, without sound, simply becoming open the way a wound becomes open, the way a mouth becomes open to let out something that has been waiting inside the throat for years. Beyond the gate: a farmhouse, its windows lit amber, and inside, a long table set for people who may or may not arrive.

The wound opens too. It has always been opening, quietly, beneath the shirt, beneath the ribs, in that place where music enters before it becomes sound. Someone is tuning an instrument in the other room. A cello, perhaps, or the ghost of one. Four chairs are arranged around the table, though only three are occupied. The fourth waits for the quartet to complete itself, the way a wound waits for the hand that will finally touch it.

She is dying at the head of the table, the woman with silver hair unraveling like unplayed notes. She lifts her spoon as though it were a bow. The soup trembles in its dish, keeping time with something no one else can hear—an adagio moving through the walls, through the wood, through the marrow of the house itself.

The gate opens again. This time it is not a gate to a farmyard but a gate to the body, and through it walks the second violin, the viola, arriving late as music always arrives late to grief, as if sound itself must first pass through wounds before it can become melody. The dying woman smiles. She has heard this quartet before, in another dinner, another dying, another gate swinging wide onto a field of wet grass and silence.

The wound opens like a door held ajar by wind. Inside it: a room where four musicians play for no audience but the dark. Inside it: the farmhouse table, the dying woman's hand reaching for bread that turns, beneath her fingers, into something like sound.

The gate opens. The wound opens. The quartet begins again, always beginning, the same four notes circling the table like grace before a meal that will never be finished, like a woman who will never quite finish dying, like a gate that will never close because closing was never its nature—only opening, only the wound's insistence on light, only the farmhouse holding its lamps up to the dark like an offering, like a chord resolving into another unresolved chord, forever almost-finished, forever ajar.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write something poetic and disjointed, almost like automatic writing, that touches on childhood, death, animals, and the idea that there's an "outside of language" beyond silence?
counterfactuals.output:
the dog under the porch knew something none of us could say
its eyes like wet stones, like the bottom of a well my grandfather
threw pennies into, wishing for what, I never asked, already
the light was leaving the kitchen the way light leaves a room
when someone has just died in it—soft, apologetic, taking
its coat off the hook on its way out

there is a place past silence. not the hush of held breath,
not the mute static between words, but a field
where the deer stand without needing to be named
deer. where my brother's crib is still warm
though he is forty now, though the doctors
turned their machines off decades ago and called it peace

I keep looking for the door in language that leads
to the thing itself—the smell of rain before rain,
the shape a bird makes right before it isn't a bird anymore
just weight, just falling, just the grass deciding to hold it

my mother hums when she doesn't know I'm listening
some tune with no name, older than the alphabet,
older than the fence I used to press my face against
to watch the horses do nothing, be nothing,
just stand there being more true than any sentence

I think death is not a silence either
it's the field on the other side of the field
the word behind the word for water

when I was young I thought if I stayed still enough
the world would show me its true shape
now I know stillness is just another kind of asking
and some doors don't open, they just
stop being doors, become wall, become sky,
become the blue nothing a bird disappears into
without translation, without goodbye
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a piece of avant-garde flash fiction/poetry hybrid that juxtaposes tender domestic scenes with violent foreshadowing (a host who will be murdered) and philosophical asides about God and isolation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Hosting

She sets out seven forks though only six will eat. This is her way—preparing for the guest who might arrive, the angel unannounced, the version of the evening that doesn't happen.

*Consider: God also sets a place for the one who never comes.*

The lamb is browning in its own fat and the kitchen smells like childhood, like her mother's kitchen, like every kitchen that ever loved someone quietly through food. She hums. The knife—she doesn't know this yet, cannot know this, the knowing is not hers to have—the knife in the block by the cutting board is not the knife that matters. That one is still three days and forty miles away, still a stranger's hand around a stranger's intention.

She folds the napkins into small white birds.

*Consider: isolation is not the absence of people but the presence of a self no one else can enter. Even God, some say, felt this—hence the making of the world, a desperate dinner party, a setting-out of forks.*

Her husband asks if she's happy and she says *ask me after dessert* and laughs the laugh that will be described later, in a small room with fluorescent light, by people who loved her, as *the last time we heard it, really heard it, before—*

Before.

The candles are lit. Outside, the night arrives the way it always does, indifferent, patient, already containing within it every hour that hasn't happened yet the way a seed contains a tree contains a table contains a woman folding napkins into birds that will not fly, that were never meant to fly, that are only paper pretending toward heaven.

*Consider: God does not warn the lamb. God only loves the shape of what is being made.*

She calls everyone to the table. Six chairs fill. One remains, terrible and empty and gleaming with its untouched fork, and she looks at it the way you look at a door you've left open out of habit, out of hope, out of some old animal faith that says: *there is room here. There is always room.*

The wine is poured. Someone tells a joke.

Somewhere, a car starts.

She will not hear it arrive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
